analysis.one_liner: Bans tax-exempt social welfare groups from spending more than 10% of their money on politics and forces big donors to be disclosed.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in July 2020 and never received a hearing or vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Some tax-exempt "social welfare" groups are allowed to spend heavily on elections without telling anyone who funded them — money that voters cannot trace, often called dark money. This bill would strip the tax exemption from any such group that puts more than 10% of its spending into political activity, and would require any such group engaged in politics to publicly name every contributor who gave $5,000 or more. It was sent to the tax-writing committee and died there.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would be able to see which large donors were behind political advertising and advocacy run through tax-exempt groups. Candidates and groups that already disclose their funding would also face less competition from untraceable spending.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters who want to trace political money

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires 501(c)(4) groups that engage in politics to disclose the name and address of every contributor giving $5,000 or more, with the information open to public inspection.

It revokes the tax exemption of any social welfare group that spends more than 10% of its total expenditures on political activity, pushing election spending out of tax-preferred, donor-hidden channels.

It defines "political intervention" broadly — including ads that name and criticize a candidate, donations passed through to campaigns, and political use of the group's resources — while carving out plain voter education and commentary on official actions.
It tightens the definition of a political organization so groups cannot easily restructure to avoid the limits.

analysis.who_pays: 501(c)(4) groups that mix civic work with election spending, and their large donors, who would lose anonymity and would have to keep political spending under 10% or give up the tax exemption. Some civic groups would bear compliance and disclosure costs.

drawbacks.text: The disclosure requirement reaches donors of $5,000 or more to a politically active group [S3], and supporters of privacy argue that naming smaller-scale contributors can expose ordinary people who back unpopular causes to harassment or pressure.

The 10% cap and the broad "political intervention" definition would apply to groups on both left and right that mix advocacy with civic work, and honest supporters would acknowledge that some genuinely nonpartisan civic activity could get swept in or discouraged by compliance costs.
Money could shift to other channels not covered by the bill, since the amendment reaches only 501(c)(4) organizations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core trade is transparency: voters learn who funds political advocacy, and a few large anonymous donors and shadow groups lose their cover. The strongest objection is that disclosing donors down to $5,000 can chill participation and expose people to retaliation, and that the 10% cap may push money into other channels rather than shrink it. On balance it is a targeted transparency measure, not a sweeping overhaul of campaign finance.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means Committee and its tax subcommittee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Golden introduced the bill on July 9, 2020.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means and to the Subcommittee on Select Revenue Measures.
The bill lists 8 cosponsors, all Democrats.
No further action appears in the record, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 without the bill advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Donors and political groups that rely on tax-exempt vehicles to spend on elections without disclosing their funding — on both political sides — are better off because the bill died. Voters gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Jared F. Golden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by a Democrat in the 116th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and never held a markup or sent it to the floor; the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 8 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republicans joined, but the Democratic-run Ways and Means Committee also never advanced it, so the record shows a partisan sponsor roster without a clear partisan fight.

industries.industry: 501(c)(4) social welfare organizations that spend on politics
industries.note: These groups' political role often depends on not naming their funders; the bill would force disclosure of large donors and cap their political spending at 10% of expenditures or cost them the tax exemption. Their interest in keeping money untraceable runs against voters' ability to see who is funding campaign messaging.

industries.industry: Large donors who give through tax-exempt groups
industries.note: Donors of $5,000 or more to politically active 501(c)(4)s would have their names and addresses made public, ending the anonymity that makes this giving channel attractive.

The bill would not ban paid political ads, but capping political spending by tax-exempt groups could reduce some volume of ad buys funded by hidden donors; media firms that sell the ads would be indifferent to who pays so long as spending continues.
